newsitem.title: UK: THE PROTEUS COLUMN - A way of insuring life.
newsitem.headline: THE PROTEUS COLUMN - A way of insuring life.

text.p: THE PROTEUS COLUMN
European and American life insurers have a knack of shrugging off bad news and bouncing back with optimistic forecasts for future business expansion.

One big advantage that life companies have over makers of tangible goods such as cars or personal computers is the long term nature of their products. If a car or a computer doesn't work or it breaks down after purchase, we expect it be replaced or repaired free of charge straightaway.

With long term financial products, it may be anything up to 40 years before the customer actually uses the product. If that life policy, endowment or pension then delivers less than expected, it's often too late to make good any shortfall.
Against this background, combined with customer ignorance and inertia, many life companies have become complacent.
However, there are signs that pressure is mounting for life insurers to change tack and focus on their customers rather than their shareholders.

Life insurers are vulnerable to attack from newcomers with a clean reputation, a strong brand image and customer service culture from another retail branch, jargon-free low cost products, and an understanding of new technology.

Faced with this threat, traditional life companies need to undergo a radical re-appraisal of their operations, and re-think policy design dating back decades which placed the emphasis on increasing shareholder value rather than serving customers.
Pressure for more transparent, customer friendly products can also be expected from the budding Asian markets, where western life companies confidently talk of massive growth potential.

As Reuters reported earlier this week (Asian culture crucial to insurance growth, March 3), western insurers will fail if they ignore the cultural differences between east and west, especially as reports of mis-selling have not gone unnoticed there.
Western companies should not assume that they have nothing to learn from Asia, which already accounts for half of all global life insurance premiums.

The Takaful concept - which takes Moslem religious sensitivities into account - has been applied to life insurance in Asia with the result that product costs are transparent and commission disclosure standard.
Some commentators believe Takaful products may spread to the west, reinforcing calls from some quarters for tigher regulation and greater disclosure.

Nonetheless, the outlook for the life industry as a whole is positive, although the successful players will have to sharpen up customer service and learn to live with smaller, possibly much smaller, margins than in the past.
